missing_spec_content.spec_text: Some atomic nuclei are unstable. The nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson says decay is spontaneous and random (introTips[0]). It never says that nuclei are unstable or that emitting radiation makes the nucleus more stable.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Activity is the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays. Activity is measured in becquerel (Bq)
missing_spec_content.why: Activity and its unit, the becquerel, are not taught anywhere. Becquerel appears only as a person's name in the intro.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Count-rate is the number of decays recorded each second by a detector (eg Geiger-Muller tube).
missing_spec_content.why: Count-rate and the Geiger-Muller tube are not mentioned.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The nuclear radiation emitted may be: ... a neutron (n).
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson covers only alpha, beta and gamma. Its title and introduction present these as the only three types. Neutron emission is never mentioned.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to apply their knowledge to the uses of radiation and evaluate the best sources of radiation to use in a given situation.
missing_spec_content.why: Uses appear only as a list in the intro ("cancer treatments, smoke detectors, carbon dating and nuclear power"). The lesson does not teach how to choose a suitable source for a given use.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: man-made sources such as the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents.
missing_spec_content.why: Nuclear accidents are not given as a source of background radiation. keyPoints[3].content lists medical uses, nuclear power stations and weapons testing only.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The level of background radiation and radiation dose may be affected by occupation and/or location.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not mention that occupation or location affect background level or dose.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Radiation dose is measured in sieverts (Sv) 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv)
missing_spec_content.why: Radiation dose, sieverts and the mSv to Sv conversion are not taught.

above_gcse.text: Note: a neutrino is also given out, but you don't need to include it at GCSE.
above_gcse.why: Neutrinos are not in the specification. The spec describes beta decay only as "a neutron turns into a proton".
This puts the neutrino into a bullet the student is asked to write down. It is beyond the spec and could lead students to include it in equations.
The spec states "The identification of daughter elements from such decays is not required."

above_gcse.text: The nucleus is still in an excited state. It releases its extra energy as a gamma ray.
above_gcse.why: Excited nuclear states are not in the spec. The spec requires only that gamma is "electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus" and causes no change in mass or charge.

above_gcse.text: Natural sources (~85% in the UK) ... Also food and drink (potassium-40) ... Artificial sources (~15%)
above_gcse.why: Percentage contributions and potassium-40 go beyond the spec. The spec requires only examples of natural and man-made sources.
The term "ion pairs" is not used in the spec. The spec requires only "ionising power".

factual_errors.text: Beta: fast electron from the nucleus. Mass 0, charge −1.
factual_errors.correction: A beta particle (an electron) has a very small mass, not zero. Its mass number is 0. The bullet should say "mass number 0" or "very small mass".

wrong_terms.text: It comes from natural and artificial sources. ... Artificial sources (~15%)
Low-level radiation from natural and artificial sources

checkpoint_mismatch.key_point: keyPoints[3] Background radiation and nuclear equations
checkpoint_mismatch.why: The correctFeedback names the daughter nucleus as "polonium-218". The key point never teaches polonium, and the spec does not require daughter elements to be identified. That part of the feedback is not supported by the key point.

not_checked: The specification text for 4.4.2.2 leaves out the alpha and beta symbols and the two example equations (shown as blanks: "may be represented by the symbol:"). I could not check the lesson's notation (⁴₂He, ⁰₋₁e) against the spec's own symbols.
Whether the Unicode superscripts and subscripts in the nuclear equations display correctly for the student.
